316.title: Exile
316.hook: since 1959 the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived in exile; a sorrow held with care
316.howItsDone: Tibetan communities in exile, centered on Dharamsala and settlements in India and Nepal, have re-founded major monasteries, schools and institutes, and many Tibetans mark March 10, the anniversary of the 1959 uprising, with prayers and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four schools, and your line, four streams. Did you notice what people shared before you noticed their differences? Day three hundred sixteen.

If you had one night to leave your home, and you could never come back, what would you carry? Not what you'd pack. What you'd carry: the songs, the recipes, the prayers your grandmother said, the way your family does things. In 1959, and in the years after, a great many Tibetans faced some version of that question. Many of the practices you've met in these two weeks, the chants, the mandalas, the teachers, reached the rest of the world because people carried them over the mountains. Today: exile.
screen: `ONE NIGHT TO LEAVE.` → `WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?` → `OVER THE MOUNTAINS, 1959.`

segments.voice: Here is the history, told plainly. Chinese forces entered Tibet, and in March 1959, after an uprising in Lhasa, the fourteenth Dalai Lama, still a young man, left the city at night. He crossed the Himalayas on horseback and on foot and reached India. Many Tibetans followed him, then and in the years after. India gave land and shelter. The hill town of Dharamsala became the Dalai Lama's home and the seat of the Tibetan administration in exile. People hold strong and very different views about Tibet's politics, and the Chinese government describes these events very differently. This lesson stays with the people and the practice. And here is what the people carried. Some texts came out on foot, in bundles. Others lived in the memories of monks, who recited them so they could be written down again. The great monasteries of Sera, Drepung and Ganden were founded anew in the fields of south India, and the debating courtyards filled with clapping and questions once more. Settlements grew in India and Nepal, and later in Europe and North America. Teachers who would never have left Tibet began teaching in cities all over the world. Tibetans speak of this loss with grief. The Dalai Lama has often said that those who drove them out are also to be held with compassion. That's the sorrow held with care: not pretending it didn't happen, not letting it turn into hatred. A tradition, carried on foot, into exile.
screen: `MARCH 1959 — A NIGHT CROSSING.` · `DHARAMSALA, AND FIELDS IN THE SOUTH.` · `MEMORIZED TEXTS, WRITTEN AGAIN.` · `GRIEF, WITHOUT HATRED.` · then, large: `CARRIED INTO EXILE.`

segments.voice: For this sit, hold them in metta. Picture Tibetans living far from the land their families came from: an old monk in south India, a teenager in a city apartment who has never seen Tibet. Silently offer them the metta phrases you learned, may you be safe, may you be well, may you be at ease. If you'd like, widen it to everyone, anywhere, who has had to leave home. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Since 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans have lived outside Tibet, carrying their practice with them: a sorrow held with care.
Your line: carried into exile. Today, name one thing from your own family or past that you'd carry anywhere, and thank whoever carried it to you. Day three hundred sixteen.

pairs: monasteries founded anew in the south

fork.setup: you're a monk who has fled with nothing but your robes. your monastery's library is gone. what do you do?
options: give up on the old teachings.

fork.reveal: some texts were carried out; others were recited by monks who knew them by heart, written down again, and the monasteries rebuilt, in exile.

trapdoor: what you thought: exile is only a political story.
what it means: a people who carried a whole tradition over the mountains, and hold their grief with care.
what a scholar hears: the exile's re-founded monasteries in Karnataka and its printing of texts helped preserve and spread Tibetan Buddhism worldwide after 1959.

317.title: The bardo
317.hook: teachings on the in-between after death; a text read aloud to the dying
317.howItsDone: In Tibetan communities a lama or trained friend often reads the Bardo Thödol aloud beside the dying and, after death, beside the body, and families hold rituals during the forty-nine days that follow; many Theravada communities hold merit-making ceremonies for the dead instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday: exile, and your line, carried into exile. Did you name something you'd carry anywhere, and thank whoever carried it to you? Day three hundred seventeen.

A favorite song. A psalm. A letter from a grandchild. In hospice rooms, near the end, families sometimes read or play something to the one who is dying. Hospice staff are taught that hearing may be among the last senses to fade. Tibetan Buddhists have a whole text for that moment, meant to be read aloud beside the dying, and then beside the body, for days afterward. It speaks directly to the person who has died, in a calm voice, telling them where they are. Today: the bardo.
screen: `A SONG, A PSALM, A LETTER.` → `HEARING, AMONG THE LAST TO FADE.` → `A TEXT READ ALOUD BESIDE THE DYING.`

segments.voice: Bardo is Tibetan for the in-between, a gap between one state and the next. Tibetan teachers describe several: the in-between of this life, of dreams, of meditation, of dying, and then, after death, the stages before a new birth. They teach that this last passage can last up to forty-nine days. First, they say, comes a moment of clear light, like a cloudless sky. If it isn't recognized, visions arise, peaceful and then fierce, and finally the mind is drawn toward a new life. The text that guides this is called, in Tibetan, Liberation Through Hearing in the In-Between. Tradition says Padmasambhava composed it and hid it, and that it was found centuries later by a treasure-finder named Karma Lingpa. In the West it's known as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, a title given by its first English editor. A lama or friend reads it near the one who has died, and its message, over and over, is simple: don't be afraid; these appearances are your own mind; recognize them, and be free. Buddhist traditions differ here, and it's worth saying who says what. The Theravada Abhidhamma teaches that rebirth follows immediately, without an in-between, though some Theravada teachers allow for one. The Tibetan schools, and some other Mahayana traditions, teach the in-between in detail, and East Asian Buddhist rites also mark forty-nine days after a death. And Tibetan teachers add one more thing: every moment is a kind of bardo. Between jobs, between homes, between one breath and the next, things loosen, and change becomes possible. In between.
screen: `BARDO — THE IN-BETWEEN.` · `CLEAR LIGHT, THEN VISIONS.` · `LIBERATION THROUGH HEARING.` · `EVERY MOMENT A KIND OF BARDO.` · then, large: `IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: This one asks for a gentle heart, so go easy. If you're willing, reflect for a moment: at the very end, what would you want read to you? A verse, a song, a few words from someone you love. Just let one thing come. You don't need to decide anything. Then let it go, and notice the small gap at the end of each out-breath, the tiny in-between before the next breath comes. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Bardo. The in-between: in Tibetan teaching, the passage between death and rebirth, and every gap where change becomes possible.
Your line: in between. Today, notice one in-between moment, a doorway, a pause in a conversation, the minute after waking, and let it be open. Day three hundred seventeen.

say nothing and leave flowers.

fork.reveal: the Bardo Thödol is read to the one who has died: don't be afraid, these appearances are your own mind, recognize them.

original.note: Tibetan bar do: the in-between, the gap between one state and the next.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Tibetan word for the afterlife.
what it means: an in-between: after death, and also every gap in life where change can happen.

what a scholar hears: bar do is often glossed 'between two'; the Bardo Thödol is a 'treasure' (terma) text, and Evans-Wentz named it The Tibetan Book of the Dead in 1927 after the Egyptian Book of the Dead.

318.title: A Tibetan day
318.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists often begin the day with water-bowl offerings and prostrations, circle temples and stupas clockwise with prayer beads, and shape each practice session with refuge and bodhicitta at the start and a dedication of merit at the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bardo, and your line, in between. Did you notice one in-between moment and let it stay open? Day three hundred eighteen, the last day of the diamond vehicle.

Early morning in a Tibetan settlement in India. A grandmother wakes before her family, washes her face, and fills seven small bowls with water on the family shrine. She lights a lamp and bows three times. Then she walks out to the temple with her beads, joining a slow river of people circling it clockwise, murmuring, turning the prayer wheels as they pass. Later she'll sit for a while at home. None of it is dramatic. All of it has a shape. Today: a Tibetan day.
screen: `SEVEN BOWLS OF WATER.` → `A LAMP, THREE BOWS.` → `CIRCLING THE TEMPLE WITH BEADS.`

segments.voice: Tibetan teachers often say a practice should be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end. Here's how that looks. It begins with refuge: turning toward the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and in Tibetan practice often the teacher too. Right after comes bodhicitta: the reminder of why, for all beings. Many people say a short traditional verse joining the two, three times. That's the beginning. The middle is the practice itself. It might be om mani padme hum on the beads, or a praise to Tara, or a visualization, or tonglen, riding the breath. Whatever it is, teachers say to do it without grabbing at results. And the end is dedication. Whatever good came from this, it's given away, to all beings, so it can't turn into a private trophy. A session of ten minutes and a retreat of three years share that same shape. Around it sits the rest of the day: water bowls and lamps, the walk around the temple, the wheels, the flags on the roof. Now look back at two weeks on the roof of the world. The diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. Turn the mind. Check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. Four streams. Carried into exile. In between. And today, the diamond day. Tomorrow the path comes down from the mountains, to wherever you live, and asks a practical question: who will you practice with?
screen: `BEGINNING: REFUGE AND BODHICITTA.` · `MIDDLE: MANTRA, TARA, TONGLEN.` · `END: GIVE THE GOOD AWAY.` · `WATER BOWLS, LAMPS, THE TEMPLE WALK.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape in miniature. For the beginning, turn your attention, silently, toward what you take refuge in, and remember why you're sitting: not only for yourself. For the middle, sit with the breath, or murmur om mani padme hum if that feels right, without chasing any result. For the end, when the bell rings, give it away: whatever good came from this, for all beings. Another day, you can stretch this shape to fifteen minutes. The bell holds the time.
A Tibetan day. Refuge and bodhicitta at the start, mantra or tonglen in the middle, and dedication at the end: good in the beginning, middle and end.
Your line: the diamond day. Give today a beginning, a middle and an end: a moment of why this morning, care in the middle, and tonight, give the good away. Day three hundred eighteen.

match.prompt: match each part of the Tibetan day.

options: write down how good it felt.

what a scholar hears: the 'three excellences' (good motivation, non-conceptual practice, dedication) frame sessions in all four Tibetan schools.

319.title: Finding a sangha
319.hook: temples, meditation centers, small groups: what to look for
319.howItsDone: Buddhists practice with a sangha at temples serving their communities, at meditation centers with weekly sits and retreats, and in small lay groups meeting in homes or online; many groups run on donations (dana).

segments.voice: Yesterday: a Tibetan day, and your line, the diamond day. Did your day get a beginning, a middle and an end? Day three hundred nineteen, and a new week.

For more than three hundred days, a lot of this path has happened between you and a screen. Early mornings, a bell, a breath. That counts. But the refuge itself makes a point about people. Of the three jewels, the Buddha, the teaching and the community, one is other people: people who sit when you don't feel like it, people who notice when you've gone missing. Today: finding a sangha.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED DAYS, MOSTLY ALONE.` → `THE THIRD JEWEL IS A COMMUNITY.` → `PEOPLE WHO NOTICE YOU'RE GONE.`

segments.voice: Sangha first meant the community of monks and nuns. Today many people also use it for any group who practice together. And they come in a few shapes. First, temples. In many cities there are Thai, Sri Lankan, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Tibetan temples, built by communities who brought the teaching with them. Many welcome visitors, and some offer meditation classes in English. You may be the only newcomer in the room, and someone may hand you a plate of food. Second, meditation centers: insight, Zen, Tibetan, with a weekly sit, a talk, and sometimes retreats. Third, small groups: a handful of people in a living room, a library, a church basement, or online, sitting together on a Tuesday night. What should you look for? Teachers who are open about where their teaching comes from. Money that's explained; many groups run on dana, freely given. No pressure to commit, buy, or cut other ties. Room to ask questions. And one simple test: after a while, do the people who've been there longest seem kinder, calmer, more honest? That's the fruit. A few practical things. First visits are often awkward: you may not know when to bow, where to put your shoes, or what the chant is. That's normal. Try a place more than once before you decide. And it's fine to visit several. This week we'll look at the admirable friend, at warning signs, at visiting a temple, and at taking refuge. It starts here. You need people.
screen: `TEMPLES, BUILT BY COMMUNITIES.` · `MEDITATION CENTERS AND SMALL GROUPS.` · `OPEN TEACHERS, CLEAR MONEY.` · `FIRST VISITS ARE AWKWARD.` · then, large: `YOU NEED PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, think about where people near you gather to practice. You don't have to know yet; just wonder. After today's session, you might look one up: a temple, a center, a small group, even one that meets online. For now, sit with the breath, and remember that somewhere, in a temple or a living room, others are sitting too. The bell holds the time.
Finding a sangha. Temples, meditation centers and small groups: a community to practice with, the third of the three jewels.
Your line: you need people. Today, look up one place near you where people practice together, and just read about it. No commitment. Day three hundred nineteen.

fork.reveal: first visits are often awkward. try a place more than once, and it's fine to visit several.

original.note: Pali saṅgha: community, assembly; first the monastic order, now often any community of practitioners.

trapdoor: what you thought: sangha means a Buddhist church.
what it means: the community you practice with, the third of the three jewels.

sources.ref: The three refuges (tisarana): Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha

320.title: The admirable friend
320.hook: Ananda says good friendship is half the holy life; the Buddha says it is the whole (SN 45.2)
320.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions treat the admirable friend, a teacher or a fellow practitioner, as central to practice, and many describe choosing good companions as part of the path itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: finding a sangha, and your line, you need people. Did you look up one place near you where people practice together? Day three hundred twenty.

Half. That was Ananda's number. Tradition remembers him as the Buddha's cousin and, for many years, his attendant: the one who carried the bowl and remembered the talks. One day he came to the Buddha with something he had worked out about the spiritual life, how much of it rests on good friends. Half, he said. Good friendship is half of the holy life. It sounds like a generous answer. The Buddha didn't accept it, and his reply is where today begins. Today: the admirable friend.
screen: `ANANDA, THE ATTENDANT.` → `HOW MUCH RESTS ON GOOD FRIENDS?` → `HE SAID HALF.`

segments.voice: The scene is in a short discourse in the Samyutta Nikaya. Ananda says, in paraphrase: good friendship, good companionship, good comradeship, this is half of the holy life. And the Buddha answers: not so, Ananda. It is the whole of the holy life. Someone with admirable friends, he says, can be expected to develop and cultivate the noble eightfold path. Then he points to himself. It's by relying on him as an admirable friend, he says, that beings are freed from birth, aging and death. The Pali is kalyanamitta. Kalyana means good, beautiful, lovely. Mitta means friend, from the same family as metta, loving-kindness, the first word of this path. So an admirable friend isn't just a pleasant one. It's someone whose goodness rubs off on you. The Buddha says elsewhere that when the mind isn't yet ripe, the very first thing that helps it ripen is an admirable friend. And in a long talk to a young householder, he describes the real friend: one who helps you when you're careless, who's the same in good times and bad, who points you toward what's good, and who is glad when you do well. So in this teaching, friendship isn't a nice extra beside the practice, something for weekends. It's the practice's ground. Who you spend time with shapes what you think, what you laugh at, what you let slide. And it runs both ways: you can be that friend for someone. The whole of the path.
screen: `HALF? NOT SO, ANANDA.` · `KALYANA, GOOD. MITTA, FRIEND.` · `THE FIRST THING THAT RIPENS THE MIND.` · `THE REAL FRIEND, DESCRIBED.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: For this sit, name one admirable friend. Someone whose goodness has rubbed off on you, alive or not, near or far. Picture their face. Remember one moment when they pointed you toward something good. Silently thank them. Then turn it around: think of one person for whom you might be that friend. Let them both rest in your mind, and then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Kalyanamitta. The admirable friend, whose goodness rubs off on you. Not half the holy life, the Buddha says: the whole of it.
Your line: the whole of the path. Today, send one short message to the friend you named, and tell them one thing they gave you. Day three hundred twenty.

match.prompt: match the pieces of the admirable friend.

myth: the Buddha agreed that friendship is half of the holy life
he said: not so, Ananda. it is the whole of the holy life.
mitta, friend, is related to metta, loving-kindness
the same family of words.
the Buddha called himself an admirable friend
he said relying on him as an admirable friend frees beings from birth, aging and death.

not so: it's the whole of the holy life.

fork.reveal: not so, Ananda. it is the whole of the holy life. someone with admirable friends can be expected to develop and cultivate the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: a good friend is a nice extra.
what it means: the Buddha calls admirable friendship the whole of the holy life.
what a scholar hears: in SN 45.2 the Buddha names himself the kalyāṇamitta; in the Meghiya Sutta (AN 9.1) admirable friendship is the first condition for the mind's ripening.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 45.2, Upaddha Sutta (half the holy life)
Anguttara Nikaya 9.1 / Udana 4.1, Meghiya (the first condition)
Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta (the true friend)

321.title: Cautions
321.hook: the Kalamas: test a teaching yourself, and trust no one who asks for secrecy or blind obedience (AN 3.65)
321.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Kalama Sutta to encourage students to test the teaching in their own experience, and many communities publish codes of conduct and financial information so that students can check a group openly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kalyanamitta, and your line, the whole of the path. Did you tell your admirable friend one thing they gave you? Day three hundred twenty-one.

Kesaputta was a town of the Kalamas, and teachers kept passing through it. Each one, the sutta says, explained his own teaching and made it shine, and ran down everyone else's. Then the next one came and did the same. The Kalamas were left with a plain, tired question: which of these people is telling the truth? When the Buddha came through, they asked him exactly that. His answer is often quoted, and often quoted wrong. Today: cautions.
screen: `TEACHERS KEEP PASSING THROUGH.` → `EACH ONE RUNS DOWN THE LAST.` → `WHICH OF THEM IS RIGHT?`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha tells the Kalamas that their doubt is reasonable. Then he gives a list, here in paraphrase. Don't go by reports, or by tradition, or by hearsay. Don't go by scripture, or by logic, or by inference, or by what merely seems plausible, or by a view you already like. Don't go by how impressive a speaker is, or by the thought, this is our teacher. Instead, when you know for yourselves that certain things are unwholesome, blamed by the wise, and lead to harm and suffering when you act on them, let them go. When you know that things are wholesome, praised by the wise, and lead to well-being, take them up. Then he asks them questions. Does greed lead to benefit or harm? Hatred? Delusion? And they answer for themselves. Notice what the sutta does not say. It isn't believe whatever feels right. It points to results you can watch in your own life, and to the judgment of wise people. Test it yourself, with your eyes open. There's a second caution, and it comes from other texts, not this one. In a short discourse the Buddha says the sun, the moon and his teaching shine openly; they aren't hidden. And near the end of his life he said he had never held back anything in a closed fist. Some traditions keep certain practices for students who have prepared, as you saw in the Tibetan weeks. That's different from secrecy about money, or about how people are treated, or demands for obedience that override your conscience. Those are warning signs anywhere. Test it yourself.
screen: `YOUR DOUBT IS REASONABLE.` · `KNOW FOR YOURSELVES.` · `WATCH THE RESULTS, ASK THE WISE.` · `THE TEACHING SHINES OPENLY.` · then, large: `TEST IT YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Before the sit, think of one warning sign you'd want to remember, in any group, spiritual or not. Maybe it's being told not to ask questions. Maybe it's money nobody explains, or being pulled away from friends. Pick one, and after the sit, write it down. Then sit with the breath, and notice something you can test right now: does this breath, watched closely, bring agitation or ease? Just look. The bell holds the time.
Cautions. The Buddha told the Kalamas to know for themselves, by results and by the wise, and his teaching shines openly, not in secret.
Your line: test it yourself. Today, take one thing you've heard on this path and check it against your own day: does it lead to harm, or to ease? Day three hundred twenty-one.

match.prompt: match the cautions to where they come from.

myth: the Kalama Sutta says believe whatever feels right to you
it points to results you can watch and to the judgment of the wise.
the Buddha told the Kalamas not to go even by scripture
scripture is on the list, alongside tradition, logic and a teacher's reputation.
the warning about secrecy comes from the Kalama Sutta itself
it echoes other texts: the teaching shining openly, and no closed fist.

fork.setup: you're a Kalama. teacher after teacher says only his way is true. you ask the Buddha whom to believe. what does he tell you?
options: believe me, not them.
know for yourselves, by results and the judgment of the wise.
believe the oldest tradition.
fork.reveal: he says their doubt is reasonable, and asks them to see for themselves whether greed, hatred and delusion lead to harm.

original.note: Pali Kālāma: the clan of Kesaputta who asked the Buddha whom to believe (AN 3.65).

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha said to trust your gut.
what it means: test a teaching by its results in your life and by the judgment of the wise.
what a scholar hears: the ten grounds not to rely on include piṭaka-sampadāna, 'the authority of a text'; the openness theme is AN 3.129 and the 'teacher's closed fist' (ācariya-muṭṭhi) of DN 16.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.129 (three things that shine openly)
Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 2.25 (no teacher's closed fist)

322.title: Visiting a temple
322.hook: shoes off, bow, sit toward the back, don't point your feet at the shrine
322.howItsDone: Visitors to Buddhist temples usually remove their shoes, dress modestly, bow or join their palms, sit toward the back and keep their feet from pointing at the shrine or monks; in many Theravada temples women do not hand things directly to monks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cautions, and your line, test it yourself. Did you check one teaching against your own day? Day three hundred twenty-two, the end of the week.

You're standing at the gate of a temple for the first time. There's a pile of shoes by the steps. Inside, you can hear a soft chant, and you can smell incense. Someone walks past you and bows. First-time visitors tend to carry the questions of a guest at a stranger's wedding: am I dressed right, where do I stand, what if I do it wrong? A handful of customs covers most of it, and a guest who's trying is usually met kindly. Today: visiting a temple.
screen: `A PILE OF SHOES BY THE STEPS.` → `CHANTING, INCENSE, A BOW.` → `WHAT IF I DO IT WRONG?`

segments.voice: Shoes off. At the door of the shrine hall, and in some countries at the gate of the whole temple, shoes come off. Look for the pile and add yours. Dress simply, with shoulders and knees covered. Inside, many Buddhists bow three times, the three bows you learned in the practices camp, to the Buddha, the teaching and the community. In Theravada temples it's often a five-point bow: forehead, forearms and knees to the floor. As a guest, you can simply put your palms together at your chest and lower your head a little. That gesture has a name, anjali, and in Thailand it's the wai. Then sit toward the back, on the floor or a chair, whatever others are doing. And the custom that's easiest to miss: don't point your feet at the Buddha image, the shrine, or a monk. In much of Asia the feet are the lowest part of the body, so pointing them is like pointing a dirty shoe. Sit cross-legged, or fold your legs to the side. A few more. In many Theravada temples, women don't touch monks or hand them things directly; an offering is placed on a cloth or passed through someone else. Walk clockwise around a stupa. Ask before taking photos. Don't touch or climb on images. Customs differ between a Thai temple, a Japanese one and a Tibetan one; when in doubt, watch and copy, or ask. Now look back at the week. Carried into exile. In between. The diamond day. You need people. The whole of the path. Test it yourself. And today: shoes off.
